question: What did the boundary commissions work from, why did Gurdaspur go to India, and what does the free record settle about the force, the dead and the displaced?
claims: The notional line and the terms of reference are in the record, the census figures the commissions argued from are in it as the members reproduce them, and every count of Gurdaspur's people in it puts the district within 2 points of half.

The award placed 4 districts across the notional line, and the only document that ties Gurdaspur to Kashmir before the award is the Viceroy's own; nothing in the free record shows it reached Radcliffe.

The force meant to hold the Punjab had, the police apart, 1 effective rifle for at least 1,600 people by its Governor's count, and the dead and the displaced are unlike counts that this thesis sets side by side and does not reduce to one number.

sentences.text: The statement read to the House of Commons when the plan was announced told the two provincial assemblies to meet in two parts, and it named the count they would be divided by: “For the purpose of determining the population of districts, the 1941 census figures will be taken as authoritative.” The Boundary Commissions were to be instructed “to demarcate the boundaries of the two parts of the Punjab on the basis of ascertaining the contiguous majority areas of Muslims and non-Muslims”, and to take into account other factors.
The Punjab commission sat in public at Lahore from 21 July to 31 July 1947, and was asked to decide before 15 August.
Its chairman signed the award at New Delhi on 12 August 1947.
This thesis asks what the commissions worked from, why Gurdaspur went to India, and what the free record settles about the force that was to hold the Punjab, the dead and the displaced.
It makes three claims.

First, that the notional line and the terms of reference are in the record, that the census figures the commissions argued from are in it as the members reproduce them, and that every count of Gurdaspur's people in it puts the district within 2 points of half.

Second, that the award placed 4 districts across the notional line, and that the only document tying Gurdaspur to Kashmir before the award is the Viceroy's own, with nothing to show it reached Radcliffe.

Third, that the Boundary Force had, the police apart, one effective rifle for at least 1,600 people by its Governor's count, and that the dead and the displaced are unlike counts, which this thesis sets side by side and does not reduce to one number.

The primary documents this thesis holds were fetched from the UK legislation and Hansard services, from the digitised Constituent Assembly Debates, from the National Assembly of Pakistan, from the United Nations document system and from scans on the Internet Archive, and every passage below was sliced from that copy by a script rather than retyped.
The two awards and the Sylhet report are held from the Government of India's own reprint, paragraph by paragraph and schedule paragraph by schedule paragraph.

Three of the four reports of the Punjab commission's members, the Muslim League's memorandum, the Governor of the Punjab's note to the Viceroy of that March, the Viceroy's press conference and the liaison agency's recovery letter are held from Kirpal Singh's documentary collection, and the pages given are the collection's. The Transfer of Power volumes are Crown copyright, so they are held only as at most five passages each, and Mountbatten's own last report is among what the cap leaves out.
The scholarship is held only as the passages cited, and one source is in Punjabi, with a rendering marked as this thesis's own.
What the record does not hold is listed under the gaps below, by name, with what was tried.

The largest are the Punjab volume of the census the commission argued from, which is known here only as the commission's members reproduce it; the report of the second League-nominated judge, which the collection carries and this pass did not slice; the two governments' submissions to the Security Council, which were fetched but whose text layers are unreadable; the one peer-reviewed demographic count of the Punjab's dead, which is paywalled; and every Urdu, Hindi and Bengali source that could be found, none of which could be read as text.
The Indian fact-finding body's own statement of the limits of counting comes first.

It wrote that the census returns of 1941 “were not accurate even at the time they were compiled”, that they became “hopelessly wrong, at the end of six years”, and that its own witnesses covered 2,094 of the 19,914 villages of West Punjab.
The Act set the appointed day as “the fifteenth day of August, nineteen hundred and forty-seven”, and set up two Dominions, India and Pakistan.
From that day the suzerainty of the Crown over the Indian States lapsed, and with it every treaty and agreement between the Crown and their rulers.
The Prime Minister told the Commons that the time given to the Bill was not commensurate with its importance and that the Government was constrained by the urgency of the matter.
In the Lords the Secretary of State said the House was being asked for a passage “so rapid as to be almost unprecedented” and that it might appear “a degree of haste that is almost unseemly”.

The plan's own instrument was the notional division: the assemblies of Bengal and the Punjab would sit in two parts according to Muslim-majority and non-Muslim-majority districts, and until a commission's report was put into effect “the provisional boundaries indicated in the Appendix to the White Paper will be used”.

The appendix lists the Muslim-majority districts by the 1941 census: in Bengal the listed districts of the Chittagong, Dacca, Presidency and Rajshahi divisions; in the Punjab the listed districts of the Lahore, Rawalpindi and Multan divisions, Gurdaspur among them.

sentences.text: The commissions did not work from surveys of their own.

Answering the commission's secretaries on 23 July 1947, Sir George Abell “did not attach the map but suggested that any map if read with the population statistics in the 1941 census would suffice for the purpose”.
The parties argued from that census, and against it.
The League-nominated judge wrote that the Muslims of Gurdaspur were 51.14 per cent of its people against 48.86 non-Muslim, and printed the four tehsils' communities from the 1941 census.

The Congress-nominated judge took the same district total of 1,153,511, with 589,923 Muslims and 563,488 non-Muslims, and set against it an affidavit on an arithmetical error in the Shakargarh register that would reduce the Muslim majority from 26,000 to 20,000.

The event record's claim that the maps Radcliffe worked from had not been resurveyed since the census before last is carried by no document this record holds, and the episode's line that he worked from the last census is.

The Punjab commission was constituted by the Governor-General's announcement of 30 June 1947, with Din Muhammad, Muhammad Munir, Mehr Chand Mahajan and Teja Singh as members and Radcliffe appointed chairman afterwards.
Radcliffe did not attend the public sittings in person, because the Bengal commission was sitting at the same time, and had the daily record sent to him.
After the sittings the commission adjourned to Simla, where the divergence between the members proved so wide that no agreed line was possible, and they assented to his giving his own decision.
The Prime Minister had told the Commons that Radcliffe “has accepted the request made to him by all parties in the Government of India to be chairman of both Commissions”.

blocks.title: The Punjab award, paragraph 9: the debatable ground
blocks.creator: Cyril Radcliffe
blocks.repository: Internet Archive, Digital Library of India collection (Government of India Press reprint, 1958)

blocks.text: 9. The task of delimiting a boundary in the Punjab is a difficult one. The claims of the respective parties ranged over a wide field of territory, but in my judgment the truly debatable ground in the end proved to lie in and around the area between the Beas and Sutlej rivers on the one hand, and the River Ravi on the other. The fixing of a boundary in this area was further complicated by the existence of canal systems, so vital to the life of the Punjab but developed only under the conception of a single administration, and of systems of road and rail communication, which have been planned in the same way. There was also the stubborn geographical fact of the respective situations of Lahore and Amritsar, and the claims to each or both of those cities which each side vigorously maintained. After weighing to the best of my ability such other factors as appeared to me relevant as affecting the fundamental basis of contiguous majority areas, I have come to the decision set out in the Schedule which thus becomes the award of the Commission. I am conscious that there are legitimate criticisms to be made of it: as there are, I think, of any other line that might be chosen.
blocks.short: Cyril Radcliffe, Chairman of the Punjab Boundary Commission, Report of the Punjab Boundary Commission (the Punjab... (1947)

sentences.text: The award names its own reasons.

Radcliffe hesitated “long over those not inconsiderable areas east of the Sutlej River and in the angle of the Beas and Sutlej Rivers in which Muslim majorities are found”, and left them to the East Punjab, in the true interests of neither State and because of “the disruption of railway communications and water systems”.
He could not preserve the Upper Bari Doab Canal undivided, or the Mandi hydro-electric scheme, and hoped for joint control by agreement.
He wrote that the award could not satisfy “sentiments and aspirations deeply held on either side” and that the means to gratify them lay in political arrangements with which he was not concerned.
Gilmartin reads the same paragraphs as a chairman who saw water as the most important of the other factors.

blocks.title: The notional line against the award, district by district
blocks.method: Every district the award's schedules name or place, one row per district, read against the Appendix to the Statement of 3 June 1947 (src-top-xi.item45), which lists the Muslim-majority districts by the 1941 census. The listed column is read from the appendix; the award column from the schedule paragraph the row cites, the districts west of the Bengal line and the remainder rule for the rest; crossed is yes where the award put a listed district wholly or mostly on the non-Muslim side or an unlisted district on the Muslim side, part where the schedule divides the district along thana lines, and no otherwise; crossed_n is 1 for yes and 0 otherwise. The result is the sum of crossed_n, the number of districts the award put across the line. No share is given, because the schedules place every other district of both provinces by remainder and the two documents let this thesis name only the 40 rows below.
blocks.finding: Of the 40 districts the appendix lists or the schedules name, the award put 4 across the notional line: Murshidabad, Khulna and the Chittagong Hill Tracts in Bengal, and Gurdaspur, three of whose four tehsils went east, in the Punjab; 5 more it divided along thana lines. The other 31 fell where the 3 June list had put them.
blocks.confidence: high for the whole districts, whose side the schedule states in words; moderate for the divided ones, where which part is larger is this thesis's reading of the thana list
blocks.against: the Bengal report itself says the parties propounded the most diverse solutions and that the province offers few satisfactory natural boundaries, so a count of crossings measures the award against the notional list, not against any alternative line; the Sylhet transfer, decided by referendum and a separate report, is outside the count

sentences.text: In Bengal the report says the province offers few satisfactory natural boundaries and that its development “has been on lines that do not well accord with a division by contiguous majority areas”.

Its questions were whether Calcutta could be divided, what territory the city needed, whether the river line could displace the Muslim majorities of Jessore and Nadia, whether Khulna could be held apart from Jessore, and to which State Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and the Chittagong Hill Tracts should go, the last with a Muslim population of only 3 per cent.
The colleagues could not agree on any of these, and the chairman decided.
The schedule leaves Murshidabad west of the line and turns south along the Khulna and 24-Parganas boundary to the sea, so Khulna went east.

Gandhi, at a prayer meeting in Calcutta after the award, deplored that “Khulna was to celebrate” its entry into Pakistan and said the award must be regarded as final “except to the extent that the ministers of the two Dominions agreed to vary it”.

In Sylhet, 8 of 55 thanas had non-Muslim majorities, and the chairman found that a division on majorities alone would leave the six non-Muslim thanas divorced from the rest of Assam and sever the railway, so he exchanged territory.
Every count of the district's people in the record puts the Muslim share a little over half, and the disagreement is over which count should rule.
The Sikh committee's note to Cripps tabled the district at 50.8 per cent Muslim by the 1931 census and called the three central districts balanced.

The Governor of the Punjab wrote, in the note he sent Lord Wavell, the Viceroy, that March, that Gurdaspur had 590,000 Muslims and 560,000 non-Muslims, that the Pathankot tehsil was predominantly non-Muslim, and that the other three tehsils had small Muslim majorities.

Asked on 4 June 1947 why the final boundaries would almost certainly differ from the provisional ones, the Viceroy answered that Gurdaspur's population was “50.4 per cent Muslims”, and that with a difference of 0.8 per cent it was unlikely the commission would throw the whole district into the Muslim majority areas.
The League's memorandum proposed a line on which every tehsil of Gurdaspur but Pathankot stayed in the West Punjab and the Ajnala tehsil of Amritsar joined it.
The League's judge put the Muslim share at 51.14 per cent and the tehsils at 52.1, 55.06, 51.3 and 38.8.

The Congress's judge answered with the electoral rolls, 74,790 Muslim voters against 81,525 non-Muslim, and asked why the plebiscite test used in Sylhet and the Frontier should not apply to a district whose population majority was 1 per cent or a little more.

blocks.title: Every count of Gurdaspur in the record
blocks.method: Every figure a fetched document gives for the Muslim share of Gurdaspur district's people, one row per figure, with the document, its census year and the side it was written from; where the document gives counts rather than a share (the Governor's 590,000 Muslims and 560,000 non-Muslims), the share is the Muslim count over the two, to one decimal. The result is the range of the column.
blocks.finding: Five documents from four sides put the Muslim share of Gurdaspur's people between 50.4 and 51.3 per cent, and no count of its people in the record puts it below half; the one count that runs the other way is of voters, 74,790 Muslim to 81,525 non-Muslim, which is 47.8 per cent.
blocks.confidence: high for the range, which is the extreme of five figures from five documents of four sides; the figures rest on two censuses, so the range spans 1931 and 1941 rather than one count
blocks.against: the Congress-nominated judge's report carries an affidavit that reduces the 1941 majority from 26,435 to about 20,000 and electoral rolls with 81,525 non-Muslim voters to 74,790 Muslim; the Viceroy's 50.4 is described by the League's judge as an error, and the Viceroy himself said 'I think' when he gave it

sentences.text: The schedule follows the Ujh river down the western boundary of the Pathankot tahsil to the point where the Pathankot, Shakargarh and Gurdaspur tahsils meet, and then the Ravi along the boundary between the Gurdaspur and Shakargarh tahsils and between Batala and Shakargarh, so Shakargarh went west and the other three tahsils east.

Lord Ismay received a message from Liaquat Ali Khan whose gist, as he restated it, was that Gurdaspur or a large portion of it had been given to East Punjab, that the report was that this was “a political decision, and not a judicial one”, and that if so it was a grave injustice amounting to a breach of faith.

Ismay answered that the Viceroy had from the outset made it clear he must have nothing to do with the commissions and that the Indian leaders had themselves selected them, drafted their terms and undertaken to implement the award.

The Viceroy's own record of an interview eight days before the award was signed has him telling the Nawab of Bhopal that Kashmir “was so placed geographically that it could join either Dominion, provided part of Gurdaspur were put into East Punjab by the Boundary Commission”.

That sentence is the only document in this record that ties Gurdaspur to Kashmir before the award, and it is the Viceroy's, not Radcliffe's. The award's reasons do not mention Kashmir, and the schedule names the State of Kashmir only as the place where the west branch of the Ujh enters the Punjab.

The two stated grounds that name Gurdaspur or its tahsils are the Upper Bari Doab Canal from Madhopur in Pathankot, which the chairman could not preserve undivided, and the Mandi hydro-electric scheme, which supplies Gurdaspur among the districts it names and which he could not keep under one jurisdiction; the passage on the Sutlej and the Ferozepore headworks concerns Ferozepore, not Gurdaspur.
Those grounds are what the Pakistani account's charge of a political decision is set against, and the award says no more of them than that.
The record therefore shows a motive on the Viceroy's side and no document that carries it to the chairman, and this thesis says no more than that.

At the end of October the Commons was told that some 2,000 armed raiders had entered Kashmir on or about 22 October, that the Maharaja had appealed to India on 26 October and asked leave to accede, and that on 27 October his accession was accepted “subject to a reference to the people of Kashmir”.

The Security Council's resolution 47 of 21 April 1948 noted that both governments desired the accession “decided through the democratic method of a free and impartial plebiscite” and recommended measures to bring it about, beginning with the withdrawal of tribesmen and Pakistani nationals.
Schofield's reading is that the plebiscite has never been held, the state remaining divided in fact between the two countries, and her paper examines why it was not held.

blocks.title: The force that was supposed to hold

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A force had been assigned to prevent this. Go back a week. The Punjab Boundary Force, under Major General Rees, was to hold the twelve districts the line would cut. On the eighth of August the Governor, Sir Evan Jenkins, telegraphed the Viceroy with the count.

sentences.text: In the first of two reports on the Force, the Governor of the Punjab told the Viceroy that its Commander put his 5 brigade groups at an average of 1500 effective rifles, “say 7500 effective rifles to control 12 districts with a population of no less than 12 million”, and that static troops and training centres would add another 1500.

In the second, a letter written the day after the award was signed, he wrote that the population of the districts was distributed over 17,932 inhabited towns and villages, that he had estimated the need at a minimum of about 20,000 effective fighting men, and gave the effective strength as about 7,500, or about 9,000 with static troops.
The episode's count of the Force is not one this record holds.

blocks.text: 5. The Commander, Punjab Boundary Force, has a most difficult task. The population of the twelve districts in which he is operating is close on 14.5 million, and this population is distributed over 17,932 inhabited towns and villages. When the possibility of the enforcement of a Boundary award was first discussed, I estimated that we should need at least two Divisions of full strength and on a War footing — i.e. a minimum of about 20,000 effective fighting men. The effective strength of the P.B.F. is at present about 7,500, or including static troops and training centres about 9,000. Now that the Police are definitely unreliable in Lahore and Amritsar, the troops have a rapidly increasing responsibility. Neither the railways nor the main roads are safe, and the village raiding is quite impossible to control without a very great display of force. Fire power is really less important than numbers.

blocks.title: One rifle for at least 1,600 people
blocks.method: The Governor of the Punjab's telegram of 8 August 1947 gives the Boundary Force's strength as 5 brigade groups averaging 1,500 effective rifles, 7,500 in all, for 12 districts with a population of no less than 12 million. One row; the result is the population divided by the rifles.
blocks.finding: By the Governor's telegram of 8 August 1947, the Boundary Force had, in addition to police, one effective rifle for at least 1,600 people in the 12 districts it was to hold: the telegram says 'no less than 12 million', so the ratio is a floor.
blocks.confidence: high: both figures sit in one sentence of one telegram, and the result is a division
blocks.against: the strength is 'in addition to police', whose numbers the telegram does not give, so the ratio counts the Force alone; the same Governor's letter of 13 August gives 14.5 million people and about 9,000 including static troops and training centres, which is one rifle to about 1,611, and 17,932 inhabited towns and villages; and he had estimated the need at a minimum of about 20,000 effective fighting men, so the ratio measures the force he had, not the force the task needed

sentences.text: The same telegram said that rural raiding in areas where the communities were inextricably mixed could not be checked except by a display and use of force on a massive scale, and said interception of raiders was vital.
What the Governor described is a force that had been asked for and counted before the line existed, and found short the day after the line was signed.

The Indian fact-finding body examined “nearly fifteen thousand witnesses” who bore testimony to the murder of “fifty thousand non-Muslims”, and said the incidents deposed to represented only a fraction of the devastation.
Taking that into account it estimated the loss of non-Muslim life “at a figure between 200,000 and 250,000”, and believed “an equal number of Muslims perished in the course of the riots in India”.

The economists write of “nearly a million deaths due to the riots” and of “a mass migration and population transfer of nearly 17 million people”, and put the displaced at “14.5 million people” within four years of partition.
The figures are set beside each other in the disagreements below, and this thesis states no single number.

blocks.title: One migration, five counts
blocks.method: Every figure the fetched documents give for the number of people displaced by the partition, one row per figure, in millions as the document states it, with the border, the period and the direction each figure counts. The result is the number of rows. No range is taken across them, because they do not count the same thing.
blocks.finding: The record holds five counts of five different things: one border by December 1947 (8.5 million), one direction by 1951 (7.3 million), both borders over four years (14.5 million), the whole transfer (nearly 17 million), and one province over twenty years (at least 6 million). The only two that count the whole transfer are the economists' own, 14.5 to 17 million, both from Bharadwaj and Mirza, the first citing Bharadwaj, Khwaja and Mian.
blocks.confidence: high for the count of rows; the 14.5 to 17 span is one producer's, and the other three are not comparable with it or with each other
blocks.against: the SGPC compilation's 'over twelve millions' and the Indian fact-finding body's warning that refugee estimates 'do not give a true picture' are both in the record and neither is a digit this table can hold; the Hansard figure is 'or thereabouts' and covers the Punjab only

sentences.text: The Commons was told in December that the number of refugees who had moved between East Punjab and West Punjab, both ways, “is 8,500,000 or thereabouts”, and the economists put the displaced at “14.5 million people” within four years.
They cite the 1951 census of India, which enumerated “7.3 million displaced persons”, of whom “4.7 and 2.55 million had come from West and East Pakistan, respectively”.
In the east the count runs on: Chatterji writes that between 1947 and 1967 “at least 6 million Hindu refugees from East Bengal crossed into West Bengal”.

Mahbub and Saba, from Dhaka, write that the violence on the eastern side was more protracted and more episodic, beginning with the Kolkata and Noakhali riots of 1946, while the west saw massacres from 1947 to 1950.
Sarla Dutta was abducted on the road with two or three other girls, converted and renamed Anwar, and kept in the house of a man with three children.
When an army search came looking for abducted girls, her abductor put her inside the seed drum, and she slid her hand through an opening and screamed; she was 13.

The two governments had decided in December 1947, as the editor of the Punjab documents summarises it, that the conversion of persons abducted after 1 March 1947 was not to be recognised and that all such persons were to be restored to their Dominions “even against the wishes of persons concerned”.

sentences.text: The Chief Liaison Officer wrote to the Chief Secretary of East Punjab at the end of April 1948 that in Sheikhupura about 100 abducted women were still to be recovered, that the District Liaison Officer had clues to 47 of them, and that from the start of April to 25 April only 16 women and 10 children had been recovered; in Sargodha about 100 women were still to be recovered, 28 of them reported to be with Pathans.
Dey reads Sidhwa's novel of abduction and recovery as showing a patriarchal ideology that turned women into mute signs, and language itself failing to articulate what was done to them.

Sherman, Gould and Ansari name refugee rehabilitation and the recovery of abducted women as the low-level state programmes through which recent work has bridged the study of high and low politics in the two new states.

Khushi Muhammad Jut, born at Aloona Tola in the district of Ludhiana and seven years old when Pakistan was created, recalled his elders saying “For generations we have been living here, how can we leave our homes?”, and then Sikh migrants arriving to press their brethren to push the Muslims out.
A friend of his father's from Jandali sent a horseman to warn them, and his father hid the family in a field near Nasrali on the land of Shadi Singh, before the attack they had been warned of.

Niamat Ali Malak, from a village in Patiala State, recalled the announcement that Pakistan had been made and people changing sides, with both communities attacking each other when they found the chance.

Bhagwant Singh Jawanda, born in 1924 in his father's village of Shanker in Ludhiana district, recalled Jinnah at Bradlaugh Hall in March 1947 telling the crowd “this is March, so march on, march on, march on!”, and Master Tara Singh advising the students at his hostel to walk in groups of 2 or 3.

adjudications.claim: The Viceroy had nothing to do with the award and kept clear of the Boundary Commissions.

It is not possible to make an accurate estimate of the total loss of life or the extent of damage to property caused by these riots. Figures computed on the population basis must, of necessity, prove extremely misleading. The census returns of 1941 were not accurate even at the time they were compiled. adjudications.claim: The allocation of Gurdaspur to East Punjab was a political decision, not a judicial one.

restsOn.text: 9. The task of delimiting a boundary in the Punjab is a difficult one. The claims of the respective parties ranged over a wide field of territory, but in my judgment the truly debatable ground in the end proved to lie in and around the area between the Beas and Sutlej rivers on the one hand, and the River Ravi on the other. He told the Assembly that the division of India and the partition of the Punjab and Bengal had been accepted and that it was now the duty of everyone to abide by it, that in his judgment “there was no other solution”, and that “You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other places of worship in this State of Pakistan”.
Nehru's motion of the same week is held in the same way.

He said the pledge was being redeemed “not wholly or in full measure, but very substantially”, and, in the Hindustani speech the Debates translate, that “Not far from Delhi, big cities are ablaze and its heat is reaching us here”.

sentences.text: No source in this record is by Radcliffe other than the awards themselves; his reasons are known here only as the awards state them.

No source in this record is a Muslim woman's own account of abduction or recovery; the one first-person account of abduction is by a girl who was converted and renamed, and the Muslim survivors are known here through an archive's summaries.
No source in this record is a district file, a police diary or a railway log of the Punjab in August 1947; the killing is known here through a Governor's telegrams, a fact-finding body and survivors.
No source in this record is the Punjab census of 1941 itself; its figures are known here as the commission's members and the Governor reproduce them.
No source in this record is a Sikh survivor's first-person testimony; the one Sikh voice in its own words is a poem, and the one Sikh testimony is an archive's summary.
No source in this record counts the dead of Bengal, or the Muslims who moved east; the eastern count is of Hindus leaving.
No source in this record is a Bengali survivor's testimony; the four testimonies held are all of the Punjab, and the eastern partition is known here through scholarship and the award.
No source in this record is a Dalit voice; the one work on caste inside the migration is paywalled, and no testimony held names caste.
No source in this record is in Urdu, Hindi or Bengali, and the one Punjabi source is a poem; every argument here is made from documents written in English.
